ana-mic-sa-j-80.why: Elastic laminae in the thick arterial media stretch as blood enters during systole. Their passive recoil maintains forward flow when ventricular ejection stops in diastole.

notes.A: The aorta needs a thick middle coat to withstand the large pressure changes during each heartbeat.
notes.B: Multiple concentric sheets of fenestrated elastin allow the wall to expand during ventricular ejection.
notes.C: Smooth muscle cells occupy the spaces between elastic sheets and maintain the extracellular matrix.
notes.D: Valves occur in many peripheral veins, whereas elastic arteries have no series of valves along their course.
notes.E: Elastic energy stored during systole drives passive recoil of the wall during diastole.

notes.A: Lymph nodes trap material arriving from tissues and bring antigens into contact with lymphocytes.
notes.B: Lacteals absorb dietary fat as chylomicrons, and lymph carries away cell debris.
notes.C: Blind-ended lymph capillaries collect excess interstitial fluid for return to the venous circulation.
notes.D: Lymphocytes develop in primary lymphoid organs and can proliferate after activation in secondary lymphoid organs.

notes.A: The hilum is the exit for filtered lymph, whereas blood-borne material is screened in the spleen.
notes.B: Afferent lymphatics pierce the convex capsule and empty into the subcapsular (marginal) sinus.
notes.C: The medulla is medullary cords of lymphoid tissue alternating with medullary sinuses.

notes.A: Hassall's corpuscles are medullary, but the thymus has no lymphoid nodules or germinal centres.
notes.B: A central arteriole surrounded by white pulp and a peripheral marginal zone identifies the spleen.
notes.C: Venous sinusoids and Billroth's cords belong to the splenic red pulp.
notes.D: Concentric layers of epithelial reticular cells form the characteristic medullary structures called Hassall’s corpuscles.
notes.E: Scattered maturing T cells give the medulla a paler appearance than the densely cellular cortex.

notes.A: Developing T cells enter from the blood, and the thymic parenchyma lacks both lymphoid follicles and incoming lymphatics.
notes.B: The dark cortex is packed with lymphocytes; the medulla has fewer.
notes.C: Connective tissue septa partition the cortex into lobules whose medullary tissue remains continuous.
notes.D: Bone marrow precursors mature into T cells here, and functional thymic tissue progressively shrinks after puberty.
notes.E: Cortical epithelial reticular cells surround perivascular connective tissue and contribute to the blood–thymus barrier.

notes.A: B cells occupy white pulp follicles, while T cells form periarteriolar sheaths corresponding functionally to a lymph node’s paracortex.
notes.B: Red pulp sinuses branch and rejoin, and elongated endothelial cells form their distinctive lining.
notes.C: In the open circulation, blood crosses the meshwork of splenic cords before re-entering endothelial-lined venous sinuses.
notes.D: Both organs have cords alternating with sinuses, although splenic sinuses carry blood and nodal sinuses carry lymph.
notes.E: Splenic cords are a reticular meshwork with macrophages that remove old red cells.

ana-mic-sa-j-22.why: Macrophages in the marginal zone and splenic cords engulf foreign material. Slits in the sinus lining chiefly test whether red cells can deform enough to re-enter the circulation.

notes.A: The spleen is the largest single lymphoid organ and contains extensive lymphoid tissue around its central arterioles.
notes.B: Red cells that become trapped in the splenic cords are removed by red pulp macrophages.
notes.C: The white pulp contains lymphocytes that proliferate and mount an immune response to blood-borne antigens.
notes.D: Reticular fibres support the splenic cords, which contain macrophages and antibody-secreting plasma cells.

ana-mic-sa-j-23.why: Lymphocyte numbers increase during development in primary lymphoid organs and during immune responses in secondary organs. The material each organ filters depends on its circulation.

notes.A: Afferent lymphatic vessels carry lymph through nodes, whereas the spleen and thymus lack this incoming route.
notes.C: Splenic red pulp macrophages remove ageing red cells, a specialised function of the spleen among lymphoid organs.
notes.D: Splenic tissue screens blood directly, whereas lymph nodes sample the lymph arriving from peripheral tissues.
notes.E: The thymic parenchyma has an epithelial cell scaffold, unlike the reticular fibre network in lymph nodes.
notes.B: Developing lymphocytes divide in primary organs, and mature lymphocytes multiply after activation in secondary organs.

ana-mic-sa-j-29.why: Brunner’s glands in the duodenal submucosa secrete alkaline mucus that helps neutralise incoming gastric acid. Their absence helps distinguish jejunum from duodenum on a section.

notes.A: Large aggregated Peyer’s patches are characteristic of the ileum, so their absence does not distinguish jejunum from duodenum.
notes.B: Intestinal crypts extend into the mucosa of both the duodenum and jejunum and renew their epithelial lining.
notes.C: The jejunum has particularly prominent circular folds, which increase the mucosal area available for absorption.
notes.E: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen in gastric glands and are absent from both of these small intestinal segments.

ana-mic-sa-j-3.why: The conchae bring air against vascular mucosa that warms and humidifies it. Most conchal mucosa is respiratory, with areas of specialised olfactory epithelium high in the nasal cavity.

notes.A: Each lateral nasal wall usually bears superior, middle and inferior bony shelves.
notes.B: The inferior concha is normally covered by respiratory epithelium that helps condition inhaled air.
notes.C: Much of the conchal surface has respiratory epithelium, but part of the superior concha bears olfactory receptors.
notes.D: Conchae increase surface area and create turbulence to warm and humidify air.
notes.E: The narrow meatuses bring air into close contact with the mucus.

notes.A: They are air spaces in the bones around the nasal cavity.
notes.B: The sinuses are frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid and maxillary; none are in the palatine or lacrimal bones.
notes.C: The sinus lining is thinner than the main nasal respiratory mucosa and contains relatively few mucus-producing goblet cells.
notes.D: Each opens into the nasal cavity by a narrow ostium.

notes.A: It is a fibromuscular half-tube, open in front to the nose, mouth and larynx.
notes.B: It carries air and food and acts as a resonating chamber for speech.
notes.C: Tonsillar lymphoid follicles and diffuse lymphoid tissue sample antigens arriving from the nose and mouth.
notes.D: Respiratory epithelium lines much of the nasopharynx, whereas non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium protects the food passages from abrasion.
notes.E: Each auditory tube opens into the lateral nasopharynx and allows pressure equalisation across the eardrum.

notes.A: It conducts air, makes sound and closes as a sphincter to protect the airway.
notes.B: It belongs to the conducting portion; gas exchange starts at the respiratory bronchioles.
notes.C: The epiglottis is elastic cartilage; the thyroid and cricoid are hyaline.
notes.D: The arytenoids are mainly hyaline; the corniculates, cuneiforms and arytenoid tips are elastic.
notes.E: Fibroelastic sheets support the folds, and intrinsic skeletal muscles alter the position and tension of the vocal folds.

ana-mic-sa-j-8.why: Within the lung, bronchi retain cartilage and mucus-producing glands. Irregular cartilage plates support the airway, while a band of smooth muscle deep to the mucosa regulates its calibre.

notes.A: Intrapulmonary bronchi retain a respiratory lining, but irregular cartilage plates replace tracheal rings and smooth muscle encircles the mucosa.
notes.B: Bronchi conduct air towards the gas-exchange regions, while their vascular lining and mucociliary clearance help warm and clean it.
notes.C: A smooth muscle layer with elastic fibres lies between the lamina propria and submucosa.

notes.A: Bronchioles are 1 mm or less and have no cartilage or glands.
notes.B: The lining becomes lower distally, with goblet cells disappearing as secretory club cells become prominent in terminal bronchioles.
notes.C: Their smooth muscle layer is relatively thick for their size.
notes.D: Club cells release protective secretions, including surface-active material that helps keep small airway surfaces apart.
notes.E: Vagal stimulation constricts bronchiolar smooth muscle, while circulating adrenaline acting at beta-2 receptors promotes relaxation.

notes.A: Alveoli open from their walls, so some gas exchange happens here.
notes.B: Cuboidal cells and club cells line the airway segments, while thin squamous pneumocytes line the alveolar outpocketings.
notes.C: Smooth muscle and elastic fibres lie between the alveolar openings.
notes.D: They lie between the terminal bronchioles and the alveolar ducts.
notes.E: Type I pneumocytes line the alveolar outpocketings, where their thin cytoplasm favours gas diffusion.

notes.A: Surfactant spreads as a thin film at the air-facing surface of the liquid lining each alveolus.
notes.B: Surface-active phospholipids reduce the attraction between water molecules at the alveolar air–liquid interface.
notes.C: As an alveolus becomes smaller during expiration, low surface tension helps prevent its walls collapsing together.
notes.D: Premature infants with insufficient surfactant have poorly compliant lungs and may develop neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.
notes.E: Type II pneumocytes package surfactant in lamellar bodies and release it onto the alveolar surface.

notes.A: Its layers include alveolar epithelium, both basal laminae and capillary endothelium.
notes.B: Its connective tissue has fibroblasts, macrophages, collagen and elastic fibres.
notes.C: At the thinnest sites, gases cross the surface lining, a type I pneumocyte, fused basal laminae and capillary endothelium.
notes.D: Connective tissue between the epithelial and endothelial basal laminae makes some regions of the septum thicker.
notes.E: The thin side offers the shortest diffusion path, while interstitial fluid can accumulate in the thicker connective tissue compartment.

notes.A: They clear inhaled particles from the air spaces and red cells from the septum.
notes.B: They work both in the septal connective tissue and in the alveolar lumen.
notes.C: Macrophages carrying indigestible pigment can persist in the septal connective tissue for long periods.
notes.D: Macrophages that ingest inhaled carbon retain dark particles visible in tissue sections, including those from smokers.
notes.E: Alveolar macrophages engulf inhaled organisms, although ingestion does not guarantee that the organism will be destroyed.

notes.A: Pigment in the epithelium and glands gives a yellowish-brown colour.
notes.B: Sustentacular cells and basal progenitors accompany the receptor neurons, while underlying glands supply fluid to the surface.
notes.C: Bowman's glands produce the serous secretion that dissolves and washes away odorants.
notes.D: Bundles of receptor-cell axons pass through the lamina propria alongside the serous olfactory glands.
notes.E: Basal progenitor cells can differentiate into new bipolar receptor neurons after birth.

notes.A: Papillae are on the dorsum; the ventral surface has thin, smooth mucosa.
notes.B: Bundles of skeletal muscle cross in different planes, allowing the tongue to change shape as well as position.
notes.C: Keratin on filiform tips gives them a whitish appearance, whereas vessels show through the thinner fungiform epithelium.
notes.D: Minor salivary glands lie among the muscle bundles and release their secretions through ducts onto the tongue.
notes.E: Filiform papillae provide friction for handling food and lack the taste buds found in other papillae.

ana-mic-sa-j-26.why: Gastric glands release acid, intrinsic factor and enzyme precursors from distinct cell types. A bicarbonate-rich mucus layer shields the surface epithelium while digestion proceeds in the lumen.

notes.A: Chief cells release inactive pepsinogen, whereas intrinsic factor comes from the acid-secreting parietal cells.
notes.B: Surface mucous cells secrete an alkaline mucus that protects the mucosa.
notes.C: Each gastric pit is a surface epithelial invagination receiving secretions from glands that open at its base.
notes.D: Parietal cells supply hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor, while G cells release gastrin and chief cells release pepsinogen.
notes.E: Rugae are folds of mucosa and submucosa that flatten when the stomach fills.

notes.A: The jejunum is wider and thicker-walled, with tall, close plicae.
notes.B: Jejunal arcades are few with long vasa recti; ileal arcades are many with short vasa recti.
notes.C: Villi become shorter and often blunter towards the ileum than the tall jejunal villi.
notes.D: The ileum has more goblet cells, and its fatty mesentery is opaque.
notes.E: Aggregated lymphoid nodules called Peyer’s patches are a prominent feature of the distal ileum.

ana-mic-sa-j-30.why: The proximal duodenal bulb usually lacks prominent circular folds, giving it a smooth outline. Farther along, barium outlines folds of mucosa and submucosa across the lumen.

notes.B: Lymphoid nodules are immune tissue and do not produce the regular contrast pattern of the circular folds.
notes.C: The proximal bulb is the smooth segment, while prominent circular folds appear farther along the duodenum.
notes.D: Villi are microscopic mucosal projections throughout the duodenum, including the bulb where the contrast outline is smooth.
notes.E: The muscularis externa is present throughout the duodenum and does not account for this mucosal folding pattern.

ana-mic-sa-j-31.why: Blood from the hepatic artery and portal vein mixes in the sinusoids and flows towards central veins. Bile flows in the opposite direction through canaliculi towards the portal tracts.

notes.A: Blood arriving by both routes mixes in sinusoids, where plasma components reach hepatocytes through fenestrated endothelium.
notes.B: Sinusoids direct the mixed portal and arterial inflow towards the central vein of each classical lobule.
notes.C: Central veins empty into larger collecting veins that join the hepatic veins and then the inferior vena cava.
notes.D: Discontinuous endothelial cells line the sinusoids, and resident Kupffer macrophages lie on their luminal surface.
notes.E: Adjacent hepatocyte membranes enclose a narrow canaliculus that carries bile towards a portal tract.

ana-mic-sa-j-61.why: The muscularis mucosae is a thin muscle layer at the base of gut mucosa. The myenteric plexus lies deeper, between the muscle layers of the muscularis externa.

notes.A: These reproductive organs contain muscle that moves their contents, but they lack the layered arrangement and enteric plexus of the gut.
notes.B: The duodenum has both structures, whereas the ureter, tongue and epididymis lack this combination of gut wall layers.
notes.C: The oesophagus has both features, whereas the urinary, reproductive and respiratory structures listed lack the characteristic enteric plexus.
notes.E: The muscle in the gallbladder wall is separate from the epithelium, and the wall lacks a distinct muscularis mucosae.

ana-mic-sa-j-62.why: Orbicularis oris forms a core of skeletal muscle within the lips. Its contraction closes or shapes the mouth during feeding and speech.

notes.A: During suckling, the lips help maintain a seal so that negative pressure can draw milk into the mouth.
notes.B: The lips change shape and come together to form particular speech sounds, including those produced with both lips.
notes.C: Contraction of the lip muscles forms an oral seal that retains food during chewing.
notes.E: Both lips and cheeks have external skin, internal oral mucosa and a core containing skeletal muscle.
